stories.headline: Chakkakomban operation not India-Pakistan war, says Keralam Forest Minister Shibu Baby John
stories.title: Chakkakomban operation not India-Pakistan war, says Keralam Forest Minister Shibu Baby John
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Thiruvananthapuram: Keralam Forest Minister Shibu Baby John on Saturday said the operation to tranquilise and radio-collar wild elephant Chakkakomban in Chinnakanal, Idukki district, was not an India-Pakistan war and that no undue pressure should be put on the officials involved or the animal.
The Forest Department had undertaken the operation to radio-collar Chakkakomban, which frequently strays into human habitations, posing a threat to people's lives.
However, the three-day effort did not succeed, following which the department temporarily suspended the operation and decided to resume it later.
John said there was no instruction to radio-collar the elephant on that particular day, and the operation was intended to be carried out in a manner that would not cause the animal stress.
The officials involved had been given the authority to make any decision necessary to ensure the mission's success, he said, adding that they decided to suspend it after three days of efforts.
The minister also urged people to understand the mental stress faced by the officials involved in the operation.

Those involved in the operation are people who work to protect elephants and forests, and they are trying to do what is possible within the available limitations to ensure the safety and lives of our people," he said.

The Forest Department, which has a responsibility akin to that of a guardian in protecting wildlife, was being forced to take difficult decisions that caused considerable emotional distress to its personnel, he said.
The minister said he had personally witnessed the mental pressure officials faced during Friday meetings with the Head of the Forest Department and the Chief Wildlife Warden.

At the same time, the safety of people living in the area could not be overlooked, he said, pointing out the potential consequences if an elephant crossed a populated area and encountered a child on the way to school.
"Setting aside our personal likes and dislikes, we are compelled to take decisions in such situations that we believe are in the larger interest of the people," he said.
The minister said the officials involved in the operation had handled the situation with considerable maturity.

stories.headline: Punjab: In election season, bitter rivals are pals again
stories.title: Punjab: In election season, bitter rivals are pals again
stories.summary: BJP old-timers fear being sidelined twice over, by the Akalis and by turncoats queuing for tickets
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: In rural Punjab they say a quarrel between relatives lasts only until the next viah (wedding) in the family.

This Gurpurab, six years after Harsimrat Kaur Badal walked out of the Modi cabinet over the farm laws, Amit Shah and Sukhbir Badal joined hands at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi, signalling the Akali Dal’s return to the NDA.
It is also said that in Punjab politics, the photo album is always kinder than memory.
Sharing the frame with Shah and Badal was Ravneet Bittu, who not long back had said the BJP could not carry the Akali burden of drugs and sacrilege.
The surprise was Shah’s generosity.
The Akalis, he said, would remain the bada bhai.
He said the farm laws, over which Akalis had walked out of the NDA, no longer mattered since they were repealed.

Sukhbir called it “not merely a political alliance, but an emotional one”, invoked his father’s bond with Vajpayee and Advani, and announced that Prime Minister Narendra Modi would come to Moga on 8 December for Parkash Singh Badal’s birth anniversary.
Both sides spoke of Hindu–Sikh brotherhood, drugs and jobs.
It was the old Punjab, Punjabi, Punjabiyat script of 1996, dusted off for a new season.
But read the fine print.
No seat-sharing formula was announced.

stories.title: Karnataka to launch ‘Delhi Chalo’ protest if Centre fails to release drought relief: Karnataka CM D.K. Shivakumar
stories.summary: The Chief Minister said the State had not received any financial assistance from the Union government for drought relief and no announcement had been made despite providing all data

He said the State had not received any financial assistance from the Union government for drought relief and that no announcement had been made on the matter.

“Even today, the Central government has not given a single rupee, nor has it announced anything,” he said, pointing out that Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara had furnished the necessary details at a special Cabinet meeting.

He had earlier participated in a meeting convened by the DMK in Chennai and said another meeting involving political parties was scheduled in Delhi.
The parties would discuss the implications of the proposed changes before deciding their position, he said.

stories.headline: Sebi working on new exchange for pre-IPO shares, consultation paper out soon: Tuhin Kanta Pandey
stories.title: Sebi working on new exchange for pre-IPO shares, consultation paper out soon: Tuhin Kanta Pandey
stories.summary: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is exploring setting up a separate trading exchange for pre-IPO shares. The market regulator is working on the proposal and plans to issue a consultation paper soon. Sebi Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the proposal is under consideration and that further details would be shared through the consultation process.Speaking at CNBC Awaaz's Market Mahakumbh event, Pandey said the idea was among the measures being examined amid the significant expansion of India's IPO market over the past three to four years. He said the regulator was considering a separate trading platform for pre-IPO shares, adding that work on the proposal was already underway.Responding to a question on whether investors could trade unlisted and pre-IPO shares on such a platform, Pandey clarified that Sebi's proposal would be limited to companies preparing to launch an IPO. The regulator does not intend to cover the entire unlisted market, which comprises lakhs of companies.Also Read | From attracting FIIs to starting Demat 2.0 accounts, Sebi chair Tuhin Kanta Pandey lists 4 prioritiesPandey also indicated that investor protection would be an important consideration while designing the proposed mechanism. He said the regulator would need to work out the framework, including safeguards for investors and additional disclosure requirements.On the scope of the proposed platform, including whether it would cover companies across market capitalisations or be restricted to a particular category, Pandey reiterated that the mechanism would be linked to the IPO process. He made it clear that Sebi would not extend the proposed arrangement to companies not connected to an upcoming IPO.The SEBI chief did not provide a specific timeline for the proposed platform but said the consultation paper would be issued soon, after which more details would become available.Sebi curbs on GMPThe development comes just days after Sebi cautioned investors against relying on grey market premium (GMP) figures, describing them as unofficial, unverified and unregulated. The regulator also clarified that investors cannot use SEBI or stock exchange grievance redressal mechanisms to resolve disputes arising from such transactions.In an advisory issued on November 23, Sebi noted that GMP figures for upcoming IPOs were being widely circulated through websites, digital platforms and newspapers. It also flagged instances of such figures being shared by certain SEBI-registered intermediaries and market participants.The regulator said these premiums are often presented as indicators of an IPO's expected listing price or potential returns, despite having no regulatory backing.Sebi to ease FII onboarding processSebi is also looking to reduce the time required for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to complete onboarding formalities from several months to as little as five business days. The move is part of a broader review of regulations governing IPOs, corporate bonds and market technology.Also Read | Sebi chairman says looking into Tata Steel-APL Apollo deal to protect minority shareholdersSpeaking at an ASSOCHAM conference in New Delhi on Friday, Sebi Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey outlined four key priorities for the regulator: simplifying regulations, deepening markets to support economic growth, facilitating access for global investors and expanding the use of technology while maintaining adequate safeguards.Pandey also said Sebi had proposed doing away with the Additional Disclosure Framework for FPIs, a move aimed at bringing India's regulatory framework closer to global standards.The proposed changes come against the backdrop of India's equity market valuation crossing Rs 500 trillion, equivalent to more than 130% of GDP. Companies raised around Rs 9 trillion through equity and debt markets in the first seven months of the financial year, including approximately Rs 1.45 trillion through 235 initial public offerings (IPOs), Pandey said.“Can it serve an economy twice its present size, finance a wider range of enterprises and remain fair, stable and trusted?” he asked, referring to the challenge facing the market.

opening: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is exploring setting up a separate trading exchange for pre-IPO shares.
The market regulator is working on the proposal and plans to issue a consultation paper soon.
body: Sebi Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the proposal is under consideration and that further details would be shared through the consultation process.
Speaking at CNBC Awaaz's Market Mahakumbh event, Pandey said the idea was among the measures being examined amid the significant expansion of India's IPO market over the past three to four years.
He said the regulator was considering a separate trading platform for pre-IPO shares, adding that work on the proposal was already underway.

Responding to a question on whether investors could trade unlisted and pre-IPO shares on such a platform, Pandey clarified that Sebi's proposal would be limited to companies preparing to launch an IPO.
The regulator does not intend to cover the entire unlisted market, which comprises lakhs of companies.
Pandey also indicated that investor protection would be an important consideration while designing the proposed mechanism.
He said the regulator would need to work out the framework, including safeguards for investors and additional disclosure requirements.

On the scope of the proposed platform, including whether it would cover companies across market capitalisations or be restricted to a particular category, Pandey reiterated that the mechanism would be linked to the IPO process.
He made it clear that Sebi would not extend the proposed arrangement to companies not connected to an upcoming IPO.
The SEBI chief did not provide a specific timeline for the proposed platform but said the consultation paper would be issued soon, after which more details would become available.
Sebi curbs on GMPThe development comes just days after Sebi cautioned investors against relying on grey market premium (GMP) figures, describing them as unofficial, unverified and unregulated.
The regulator also clarified that investors cannot use SEBI or stock exchange grievance redressal mechanisms to resolve disputes arising from such transactions.
In an advisory issued on November 23, Sebi noted that GMP figures for upcoming IPOs were being widely circulated through websites, digital platforms and newspapers.
It also flagged instances of such figures being shared by certain SEBI-registered intermediaries and market participants.
The regulator said these premiums are often presented as indicators of an IPO's expected listing price or potential returns, despite having no regulatory backing.

Sebi to ease FII onboarding processSebi is also looking to reduce the time required for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to complete onboarding formalities from several months to as little as five business days.
The move is part of a broader review of regulations governing IPOs, corporate bonds and market technology.

Speaking at an ASSOCHAM conference in New Delhi on Friday, Sebi Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey outlined four key priorities for the regulator: simplifying regulations, deepening markets to support economic growth, facilitating access for global investors and expanding the use of technology while maintaining adequate safeguards.
Pandey also said Sebi had proposed doing away with the Additional Disclosure Framework for FPIs, a move aimed at bringing India's regulatory framework closer to global standards.
The proposed changes come against the backdrop of India's equity market valuation crossing Rs 500 trillion, equivalent to more than 130% of GDP.

Companies raised around Rs 9 trillion through equity and debt markets in the first seven months of the financial year, including approximately Rs 1.45 trillion through 235 initial public offerings (IPOs), Pandey said.
“Can it serve an economy twice its present size, finance a wider range of enterprises and remain fair, stable and trusted?” he asked, referring to the challenge facing the market.

In an advisory issued on November 23, Sebi noted that GMP figures for upcoming IPOs were being widely circulated through websites, digital platforms and newspapers.
The proposed changes come against the backdrop of India's equity market valuation crossing Rs 500 trillion, equivalent to more than 130% of GDP.

stories.headline: India's FY28 fiscal deficit projected to stay unchanged at 4.3% of GDP: Deutsche Bank
stories.title: India's FY28 fiscal deficit projected to stay unchanged at 4.3% of GDP: Deutsche Bank
stories.summary: Deutsche Bank warns FY28 consolidation faces rising pay, subsidies and oil-linked costs, even as cushions keep the deficit at 4.3% of GDP
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India's fiscal deficit for the financial year 2028 is projected to remain unchanged at 4.3 per cent of GDP as expenditure pressures challenge consolidation efforts, according to a Deutsche Bank Research report.
While the central government is on track to meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.3 per cent of GDP in FY27, the path forward presents steeper hurdles.
"The central government will most likely meet its FY27 fiscal deficit target of 4.3% of GDP; however, FY28 consolidation looks considerably more challenging.
Considering the various risks, we forecast the FY28 fiscal deficit to remain unchanged at 4.3% of GDP," the report stated.

Several cushions support the government's fiscal math in the current fiscal year, including a substantial Reserve Bank of India dividend of ₹2.9 lakh crore, an ₹1 lakh crore Economic Stabilisation Fund provision, potential capital expenditure compression, and higher-than-expected disinvestment receipts.
However, the subsequent fiscal year faces headwinds from persistently elevated oil prices, larger subsidy bills, a potentially lower central bank dividend, and the rollout of the 8th Pay Commission.
"Implementation of the 8th Pay Commission, which could add at least ₹3 lakh crore to expenditure.
Delaying the pay award to 2028 could provide near-term relief but would merely shift the burden forward through a larger accumulation of arrears," the report noted.
Despite fiscal and external challenges, the report maintains a steady view on economic expansion.
Real GDP growth is projected at 7.3 per cent year-on-year in FY27, 7.2 per cent in FY28, and 7.3 per cent in FY29.

Although a sub-normal monsoon, higher oil prices, and unfavourable base effects from last year's GST rate cuts are expected to moderate growth in the second half of FY27, the implementation of pay commission awards is anticipated to lift domestic demand next year.
"We remain broadly constructive on India's growth trajectory and general resilience of the economy despite the ongoing West Asia crisis and a sub-normal monsoon this year," the report added.

stories.headline: Tata Trusts row: Tata Sons moves Bombay High Court, Supreme Court with caveats ahead of meeting
stories.title: Tata Trusts row: Tata Sons moves Bombay High Court, Supreme Court with caveats ahead of meeting
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Tata Sons, the principal holding company of the Tata group, has filed caveats before the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court in connection with the interim order passed by the Bombay High Court on November 27.

The move comes amid speculation that Tata Trusts, which hold 66 per cent stake in Tata Sons, may challenge the single-judge order before a division bench of the Bombay High Court or the Supreme Court.
The caveats were filed late on November 27 and cover proceedings before both the division bench of the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court, legal sources said.
A caveat is filed to ensure that a party is given an opportunity to be heard before a court passes any order on a petition or application filed by the opposing party.
The single bench of the Bombay High Court on Friday refused to grant any interim relief to the trusts, allowing the Tata Sons board meeting, scheduled for November 30, to go ahead.
However, any resolutions passed at the meeting will remain subject to the outcome of the proceedings before the court, which fixed January 21, 2027, as the next date of hearing.
“We are not granting any relief today.

Let the meeting go on as scheduled and everything will be subject to the outcome,” Justice Abhay Ahuja said, making it clear that decisions taken by the Tata Sons board would be subject to further orders of the court.

The Tata group battle on Thursday moved to the Bombay High Court, with Tata Trusts seeking to challenge the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for another five-year term through the casting vote, alleging that the resolution passed by the company’s board on September 17 was ultra vires its Articles of Association and therefore null and void.

Tata Trusts maintained that the reappointment resolution based on the casting vote of the chairman of board meeting – Harish Manwani — was legally invalid because the Articles of Association require the affirmative vote of a majority of the Trusts’ nominee directors for a decision on the appointment or reappointment of the chairman.
Noel Tata voted against the resolution, while Venu Srinivasan supported it.

The trusts sought interim orders restraining Tata Sons and its directors from acting upon the resolution and from passing board resolutions over the objection of either of the two Trust-nominated directors where the affirmative vote of a majority of Trust directors is required.

stories.headline: Supreme Court refuses to entertain plea to reduce minimum age for contesting elections
stories.title: Supreme Court refuses to entertain plea to reduce minimum age for contesting elections
stories.summary: When the bench observed that it was not an appropriate petition, the counsel said, ‘The respondent can just inform the petitioner what is the outcome of his representation’
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Saturday (November 28, 2026) refused to entertain a plea seeking to reduce the minimum age for contesting parliamentary and state legislature elections.

The counsel appearing for the petitioner told a bench comprising Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh that while the voting age was reduced from 21 to 18, the minimum age to be a member of the Lok Sabha is 25 and 30 for the Rajya Sabha.
The counsel also referred to the minimum age to be a member of the state legislative assembly and state legislative council.
"In this petition, there is a small but very vital issue.
The voting age, by the (Constitution) sixty-first amendment, was reduced from 21 to 18," the counsel said.
When the bench observed that it was not an appropriate petition, the counsel said, "The respondent can just inform the petitioner what is the outcome of his representation."
"For that, you go to the high court under (Article) 226 for getting a direction for deciding your representation," the bench said.
The plea had made the Centre and the Election Commission as party respondents.
The counsel then said that he would like to withdraw his plea.
"Dismissed as withdrawn," the bench said.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on November 27 extended the interim bail granted to Khalid Saifi and Tasleem Ahmed, who are accused in the 2020 Delhi riots larger conspiracy case.
They were earlier granted interim bail for 6 months, which has now been extended by 3 more months.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders Karthigai Deepam to be lit at ‘deepathoon’ on November 28; issues contempt notice
stories.title: Supreme Court orders Karthigai Deepam to be lit at ‘deepathoon’ on November 28; issues contempt notice
stories.summary: Bench directs Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, DGP, Madurai District Collector, temple authorities to be present for next hearing on Dec. 15; court sees ‘pre-meditated conspiracy' between State and temple trustees
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Rejecting the Tamil Nadu government’s claim that it stayed aloof from the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple management’s customary decisions, the Supreme Court on Friday (November 27, 2026) said non-compliance with its November 20 order to light the Karthigai Deepam at the deepathoon (stone pillar) atop the Thirupparankundram hill in Madurai amounted to “wilful disobedience” born of a “pre-meditated conspiracy” between the State and the temple trustees.

A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi ordered the Board of Trustees of the temple to be suspended before appointing two former High Court judges – former Chief Justice of Meghalaya High Court S. Vaidyanathan and former Madras High Court judge Justice V. Parthiban - to act as Receivers.
The court directed the Karthigai Deepam to be lit again on Saturday (November 28, 2026), this time on the stone pillar, as was originally ordered on November 20.
Central forces would provide security.
The Receivers have to ensure the ceremony is carried out in consultation with the temple stanikars.
However, the interim order would not grant any future equities in favour of any party.
The court made clear that its order was limited only to contempt petitions.
The main case on religious rights concerning the Thirupparankundram lamp-lighting row would be heard in the second week of January 2027.
The row stems from the claims of ownership over the hilltop.
The deepathoon is located near the Sikandar Badusha Dargah on top of the hill, while the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple is at the base of the hill.
The dargah side has claimed ownership of the hilltop, including the deepathoon site.
The court order comes two days after the ceremonial lamp was lit at the customary location – Deepa Mandapam – atop the hill and not as the Bench mandated.

stories.headline: 13-member panel to light Tirupparankundram lamp at 5 pm in Tamil Nadu
stories.title: 13-member panel to light Tirupparankundram lamp at 5 pm in Tamil Nadu
stories.summary: Madurai (Tamil Nadu), Nov 28 : A 13-member steering committee comprising retired judges, senior administrative officials, security personnel, and temple priests will oversee the lighting of the ceremonial lamp at the Deepathoon atop the Tirupparankundram Murugan temple hill in Tamil Nadu’s Madurai district at 5 p.m. on Saturday, in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directive. The committee includes retired judges Vaidyanathan and Parthiban, Madurai District Collector Nishant Krishna, the City Police Commissioner, the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) Inspector General and temple priests. Elaborate security arrangements have been put in place across Tirupparankundram and its surrounding areas, with an additional 400 CRPF personnel arriving to ensure the smooth conduct of the religious ceremony. Central security personnel have been conducting extensive searches on the hill and in adjoining areas as part of precautionary measures. Police deployment has also been strengthened in view of the anticipated influx of devotees. Earlier in the day, retired judges Vaidyanathan and Parthiban, appointed to facilitate the implementation of the Supreme Court’s order, visited the Tirupparankundram Murugan temple and offered prayers. Following special rituals at the temple, the retired judges proceeded towards the hilltop carrying the ceremonial lamp as preparations for the lighting ceremony were completed. The judges also held consultations with the hereditary temple priests, who traditionally perform religious rituals at the Murugan temple. The Madurai District Collector, District Superintendent of Police and other senior officials participated in the discussions. Meanwhile, devotees began gathering at Tirupparankundram from the early hours of Saturday, with authorities expecting a substantial turnout for the much-awaited ceremony. The Health Department has deployed 16 medical teams, including eight mobile medical units, to provide emergency assistance to devotees. Four motorcycle-based medical teams have also been stationed to facilitate rapid access to congested areas, while eight ambulances have been kept on standby to transport patients requiring emergency treatment. Authorities have advised elderly people, children, pregnant women and those suffering from cardiac ailments to refrain from climbing the hill as a precautionary measure. Tirupparankundram, regarded as the first of the six sacred abodes of Lord Murugan, has been at the centre of a prolonged legal controversy over the lighting of the ceremonial lamp at the hilltop stone pillar. Saturday’s ceremony assumes significance following the Supreme Court’s intervention, with the administration focusing on ensuring compliance with the judicial directive while maintaining public order and communal harmony. ( IANS)

stories.headline: 'Well-Researched Constructive Criticism of Judiciary Is Necessary & Welcome': Chief Justice M.S. Sonak Retires From Jharkhand High Court
stories.title: 'Well-Researched Constructive Criticism of Judiciary Is Necessary & Welcome': Chief Justice M.S. Sonak Retires From Jharkhand High Court
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in title weight 42
article_sentences: Chief Justice M.S. Sonak has retired from the Jharkhand High Court, reflecting on the importance of judicial humility, constructive criticism and the need for judges to look beyond legal pleadings to recognise the human suffering underlying every dispute.

In his farewell speech, Chief Justice Sonak emphasised that the judiciary as an institution is far greater than the individuals who serve it, and that judges must remain conscious of their constitutional responsibility to administer justice with compassion and equity.
“This entire experience of working with you all and for this great institution of ours has been very humbling.
The judiciary in general, and the Jharkhand High Court, which we were sworn in to serve, are far greater than individuals like me, who are but birds of passage.”

Reflecting on the history and legacy of the institution, Chief Justice Sonak acknowledged the contributions of the legal luminaries associated with the Jharkhand High Court and its predecessor, the Patna High Court.
“As I expressed, when demitting my office as a judge of the Bombay High Court, all told, I am not very comfortable with the general idea of praising judges for doing their judicial duties.
No one deserves praise for doing what he or she ought to do.”
“Therefore, well-researched and constructive criticism and course correction are welcome, and I should say, necessary.

But this should not be to run down the institution or its judges, but out of genuine concern that our institution fulfils the noble role assigned to it by our Constitution and that we all remain faithful to the oath we take before assuming office.”
“What always remains within our grasp, however, is to remain conscious that behind the mass of case papers thrust before us is a human face crying for justice.
Our endeavour must be to see whether we can, within the four corners of the law, do justice to that human.”

“Our endeavour must be to look beyond the cold print of a petition to the human face behind it, remembering that our constitutional duty is not merely to apply the law mechanically, but to administer justice with compassion and equity.”

stories.headline: How Adani’s next aviation move is taking shape
stories.title: How Adani’s next aviation move is taking shape
stories.summary: Talks of Adani running an airline have taken off again, with the group's CFO saying on November 27 that plans are in the making to put money in an airline if the govt allows.Coming amid a major flux in India's skies, Adani Group's statement has set aviation circles abuzz.The group has sought govt permission to invest in airlines, either by backing an existing carrier, financing a startup or backing an entrepreneur. This follows an express denial -- issued a few months earlier -- of any such ambitions.Also read | Air India’s new CEO announces $650 million cost-cutting plan with flight reshuffle, dept mergersThis development occurs at a critical time for Indian aviation.The airline business' ambitions have grown faster than its ability to give passengers enough choices. This is becoming more and more painfully clear as airline after airline fails, letting the business become a duopoly, greatly inconveniencing flyers and raising policymakers' hackles.Even as airports expand, aircraft orders swell and millions prepare to fly rather than take the train, India's skies largely remain under two companies' control. Now that the possibility rises of a third player entering the game, all focus has shifted to a company which has spent years building its presence on the ground but now wants a bigger stake in what happens above it.For India's flyers, there could hardly be any better news than a new, well-funded airline.The collapse of competition into a duopoly has made the sector significantly vulnerable to disruptions. To add to these woes, the sheer size & scale of IndiGo and Air India are making it hard for others players to remain in business, Bloomberg reported in September.According to aviation industry data, IndiGo now has a ~63–66% share and the Air India Group has ~26–28%, while smaller carriers like SpiceJet face deep trouble.The government has itself called for more airlines, with Aviation minister Naidu saying a while ago that India needs at least five carriers with fleets of 100 aircraft each.The regulatory wallDespite its July 2026 denial, Adani Group's aviation amibitions have been well-known for some time. But these ambitions have taken their own sweet time in making any kind of headway.The biggest obstacle has been not a lack of capital or any such thing, but some of India's airport rules.The operation, management and development agreements (OMDAs) for Mumbai and Delhi airports have cross-ownership restrictions. The rules are designed to prevent airlines from controlling airport operations and potentially disadvantaging rival carriers.These provisions effectively stop airport operators and their group entities from investing in scheduled airlines.Also read | Adani seeks government nod to invest in airlines, eyes bigger role in India's aviation marketAdani Airport Holdings, which controls Mumbai airport, had sought a waiver and clarification of these curbs. The govt confirmed some time ago that the Airports Authority of India got a request to that effect.However, a look-in from the Aviation Ministry remains pending, according to the govt's last information on the matter to Parliament. Any change in the situation will likely require legal scrutiny and Cabinet approval, ET reported in August.Among the factors that have clouded Adani's prospects are: contractual restrictions, competition concerns, financial demands and the risk of favouring its own airline at airports.A middle path to the skiesIt is in this context that Adani Group may have retouched its plans, with the original (July) denial now giving way to a strategy that has been tweaked with a nuance.Rather than directly seeking to start an airline from scratch, the CFO's November 27 statement said the group was looking at funding an airline or an entrepreneur willing to start one.This could give Adani a way into aviation without necessarily operating an airline itself.Adani already has significant aviation footprint. The group operates eight airports -- including Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Lucknow and Guwahati -- and handles more than a fourth of India's air passenger traffic (~96 million passengers at present, targeting 200 million).It also has interests in ground handling, maintenance, repair and overhaul and pilot training.According to an ET report, an airline investment could connect these businesses, while giving it exposure to passenger growth and aircraft operations.The group also has another reason to look skyward.It has made a partnership with Brazilian aircraft maker Embraer to explore a regional aircraft manufacturing ecosystem in India, including a possible final assembly line.The proposed venture would cover aircraft production, supply chains and related aviation services. A domestic airline investor could potentially create demand for such aircraft, although the manufacturing venture and airline investment remain separate propositions and neither guarantees commercial success, Reuters reported at the time of the deal's signing.A policy minefieldThe govt's dilemma is not small either.Allowing airport owners to invest in airlines could bring fresh capital and competition into a market where IndiGo and the Air India Group command roughly 90% of domestic traffic.But airport operators also control facilities that are critical to airlines. These include landing slots, terminal access, parking, ground services and other infrastructure.An airline owned by the airport company could very well get preferential treatment. No marks for guessing where that leaves competitors.As Adani Airport Holdings Ltd (AAHL) prepares for an FY28 demerger, the question that is being asked is: Can India’s largest private airport operator also act as a financier to an airline using its own terminals?This is the primary competition concern behind restrictions on cross-ownership, Bloomberg reported in September.By reframing the plan, Adani could be testing a middle path around India’s cross-ownership hurdles, analysts said. The basic idea could be that investing through a fund, minority stake or independent entrepreneur rather than directly operating an airline could lessen the friction, they added.But changing the funding structure may not automatically help Adani find a way around the curbs.This is particularly true in case the investment is controlled by, associated with or effectively backed by the airport operator. In such a case, regulators will have to look into ownership, control and safeguards -- and not just the name of the investor.Pockets deep, but risks high tooFew ever doubt that Adani has the financial clout to run an airline.There is one key point to note, though. An airline will add a capital-intensive business with uncertain returns to an already ambitious expansion plan.The group plans investments of Rs 2.2 lakh crore in FY27 and borrowings of Rs 1.3-1.4 lakh crore annually across the current and next fiscal years.Its consolidated debt stood at $43.2 billion at September-end, with cash of about $8 billion, ET reported in November.These numbers show major financial capacity. But they also show competing demands for capital. That is where an airline can become a tricky business addition. An airline would require sustained funding for aircraft, fuel, staff, maintenance, marketing and operations, besides absorbing losses during its early years.From Jet Airways to Go First and many others, India's aviation history is littered with failed carriers. It shows how difficult it has been to turn passenger growth into profits.As per a Bloomberg report, Adani's infra chops and ready access to capital could be an advantage. These, however, won't make up for the thin margins, volatile fuel prices and other operational risks that make life tough for aviation players, it said.

opening: Talks of Adani running an airline have taken off again, with the group's CFO saying on November 27 that plans are in the making to put money in an airline if the govt allows.
Coming amid a major flux in India's skies, Adani Group's statement has set aviation circles abuzz.
body: The group has sought govt permission to invest in airlines, either by backing an existing carrier, financing a startup or backing an entrepreneur.
This follows an express denial -- issued a few months earlier -- of any such ambitions.
Also read | Air India’s new CEO announces $650 million cost-cutting plan with flight reshuffle, dept mergers.
This development occurs at a critical time for Indian aviation.
The airline business' ambitions have grown faster than its ability to give passengers enough choices.
This is becoming more and more painfully clear as airline after airline fails, letting the business become a duopoly, greatly inconveniencing flyers and raising policymakers' hackles.
Even as airports expand, aircraft orders swell and millions prepare to fly rather than take the train, India's skies largely remain under two companies' control.

Now that the possibility rises of a third player entering the game, all focus has shifted to a company which has spent years building its presence on the ground but now wants a bigger stake in what happens above it.
For India's flyers, there could hardly be any better news than a new, well-funded airline.
The collapse of competition into a duopoly has made the sector significantly vulnerable to disruptions.
To add to these woes, the sheer size & scale of IndiGo and Air India are making it hard for others players to remain in business, Bloomberg reported in September.
According to aviation industry data, IndiGo now has a ~63–66% share and the Air India Group has ~26–28%, while smaller carriers like SpiceJet face deep trouble.
The government has itself called for more airlines, with Aviation minister Naidu saying a while ago that India needs at least five carriers with fleets of 100 aircraft each.
The regulatory wall.
Despite its July 2026 denial, Adani Group's aviation amibitions have been well-known for some time.
But these ambitions have taken their own sweet time in making any kind of headway.
The biggest obstacle has been not a lack of capital or any such thing, but some of India's airport rules.
The operation, management and development agreements (OMDAs) for Mumbai and Delhi airports have cross-ownership restrictions.
The rules are designed to prevent airlines from controlling airport operations and potentially disadvantaging rival carriers.
These provisions effectively stop airport operators and their group entities from investing in scheduled airlines.

Also read | Adani seeks government nod to invest in airlines, eyes bigger role in India's aviation marketAdani Airport Holdings, which controls Mumbai airport, had sought a waiver and clarification of these curbs.
The govt confirmed some time ago that the Airports Authority of India got a request to that effect.
However, a look-in from the Aviation Ministry remains pending, according to the govt's last information on the matter to Parliament.
Any change in the situation will likely require legal scrutiny and Cabinet approval, ET reported in August.
Among the factors that have clouded Adani's prospects are: contractual restrictions, competition concerns, financial demands and the risk of favouring its own airline at airports.
A middle path to the skies.
It is in this context that Adani Group may have retouched its plans, with the original (July) denial now giving way to a strategy that has been tweaked with a nuance.
Rather than directly seeking to start an airline from scratch, the CFO's November 27 statement said the group was looking at funding an airline or an entrepreneur willing to start one.
This could give Adani a way into aviation without necessarily operating an airline itself.
Adani already has significant aviation footprint.

The group operates eight airports -- including Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Lucknow and Guwahati -- and handles more than a fourth of India's air passenger traffic (~96 million passengers at present, targeting 200 million).
It also has interests in ground handling, maintenance, repair and overhaul and pilot training.
According to an ET report, an airline investment could connect these businesses, while giving it exposure to passenger growth and aircraft operations.
The group also has another reason to look skyward.
It has made a partnership with Brazilian aircraft maker Embraer to explore a regional aircraft manufacturing ecosystem in India, including a possible final assembly line.
The proposed venture would cover aircraft production, supply chains and related aviation services.

A domestic airline investor could potentially create demand for such aircraft, although the manufacturing venture and airline investment remain separate propositions and neither guarantees commercial success, Reuters reported at the time of the deal's signing.
A policy minefield.
The govt's dilemma is not small either.
But airport operators also control facilities that are critical to airlines.
These include landing slots, terminal access, parking, ground services and other infrastructure.
An airline owned by the airport company could very well get preferential treatment.
No marks for guessing where that leaves competitors.

As Adani Airport Holdings Ltd (AAHL) prepares for an FY28 demerger, the question that is being asked is: Can India’s largest private airport operator also act as a financier to an airline using its own terminals?
This is the primary competition concern behind restrictions on cross-ownership, Bloomberg reported in September.
By reframing the plan, Adani could be testing a middle path around India’s cross-ownership hurdles, analysts said.
The basic idea could be that investing through a fund, minority stake or independent entrepreneur rather than directly operating an airline could lessen the friction, they added.
But changing the funding structure may not automatically help Adani find a way around the curbs.
This is particularly true in case the investment is controlled by, associated with or effectively backed by the airport operator.
In such a case, regulators will have to look into ownership, control and safeguards -- and not just the name of the investor.
Pockets deep, but risks high tooFew ever doubt that Adani has the financial clout to run an airline.
There is one key point to note, though.
An airline will add a capital-intensive business with uncertain returns to an already ambitious expansion plan.
The group plans investments of Rs 2.2 lakh crore in FY27 and borrowings of Rs 1.3-1.4 lakh crore annually across the current and next fiscal years.
Its consolidated debt stood at $43.2 billion at September-end, with cash of about $8 billion, ET reported in November.
These numbers show major financial capacity.
But they also show competing demands for capital.
That is where an airline can become a tricky business addition.
An airline would require sustained funding for aircraft, fuel, staff, maintenance, marketing and operations, besides absorbing losses during its early years.
From Jet Airways to Go First and many others, India's aviation history is littered with failed carriers.
It shows how difficult it has been to turn passenger growth into profits.
As per a Bloomberg report, Adani's infra chops and ready access to capital could be an advantage.
These, however, won't make up for the thin margins, volatile fuel prices and other operational risks that make life tough for aviation players, it said.

stories.headline: World Landslide Forum Concludes in India, Calls for Science-Driven Disaster Prevention
stories.title: World Landslide Forum Concludes in India, Calls for Science-Driven Disaster Prevention
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: FARIDABAD: The Seventh World Landslide Forum (WLF7) concluded on Friday at Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham in Faridabad, with scientists and policymakers calling for greater integration of scientific knowledge into development planning and disaster prevention amid growing risks from extreme rainfall, infrastructure expansion and changing land-use patterns.

Held in India for the first time, the international forum brought together scientists, engineers, policymakers and disaster management practitioners to discuss ways to develop in geologically fragile regions without increasing disaster vulnerability, said a press release.

Organised under the aegis of the International Consortium on Landslides (ICL) and the International Programme on Landslides (IPL), in collaboration with UNESCO and other international organisations, the forum received over 700 research papers and abstracts involving nearly 1,900 authors from 75 countries and regions.

Held in India for the first time, the international forum brought together scientists, engineers, policymakers and disaster management practitioners to discuss ways to develop in geologically fragile regions without increasing disaster vulnerability, said a press release.

stories.title: FSSAI sanctions prosecution against Bisleri in another case; bacteria found in Bengal sample

article_sentences: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after a packaged drinking water sample from its Jalpaiguri plant tested positive for coliform bacteria, sources said.

New Delhi: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a packaged drinking water sample collected from its West Bengal plant failed laboratory testing, sources said.
The sample tested positive for coliform bacteria, they added.
Coliform bacteria can enter water systems through sewage leaks or damaged pipes, among other pathways.
According to sources, this is the second instance of the FSSAI sanctioning prosecution against Bisleri International, a leading player in the country’s packaged drinking water sector.
On Sunday, the FSSAI announced similar legal proceedings after a sample from one of Bisleri’s plants in Goa also failed testing.
The West Bengal sample was collected from a plant in Telipara village of Jalpaiguri.
The presence of coliform bacteria was confirmed by both primary and referral laboratories.
Consequently, the FSSAI prohibited the sale of only one specific batch, PB 201, on August 12, 2026, sources said.
According to sources, the FSSAI granted “sanction for prosecution” against Bisleri International in view of alleged violations of food safety rules.
Responses from the FSSAI and Bisleri International could not be ascertained immediately.
In the Goa case, the FSSAI had said the “sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006.”

stories.headline: EC to redraw PoK constituencies under proposed Delimitation Bill
stories.title: EC to redraw PoK constituencies under proposed Delimitation Bill
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 28 : A provision in the proposed Delimitation Bill, 2026, allows the Election Commission to undertake delimitation of constituencies in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), once they cease to remain under Pakistan's control, according to a report. The government is planning to introduce the legislation in Parliament on Monday. According to a clause in the proposed Bill, the Election Commission may facilitate the delimitation of constituencies "in the Legislative Assembly of the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir falling under the occupation of Pakistan, whenever the area ceases to be so occupied". Under the existing arrangement, the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has a total strength of 90 elected seats, while 24 seats earmarked for Pakistan-occupied Kashmir will continue to remain vacant. The proposed provision provides for delimitation in these areas if they come out of Pakistan's occupation in the future. The proposed legislation comes amid the government's broader plan to undertake delimitation and implement 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. Ahead of a special sitting of Parliament next week, the Union Cabinet on Friday cleared a Constitution amendment Bill linked to the proposed changes in the composition of legislatures and women's reservation. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-Second Amendment) Bill, 2026, was approved at the Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The proposed amendment provides for increasing the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha to 850 members and that of state legislative Assemblies by 650 members. The Bill seeks to amend Article 334A, which deals with reservation for women in legislatures. It proposes adding a proviso to increase the number of seats allocated to each state and Union Territory in the Lok Sabha, as well as the number of seats in their respective legislative Assemblies, by 50 per cent of the existing strength. This provision is understood to address a key demand raised by some regional parties regarding the proposed expansion of legislative representation. ( IANS)
